title: Unwell / Fever in a Returned Traveller (Acute Hepatitis A)
patient_instructions: You are Tom, 34, who feels generally unwell and has come in mainly to get another medical certificate for work; a colleague gave you one three days ago. You are a little impatient and initially say 'I just need another certificate, that's all.' If the doctor agrees to provide it and asks to check a few things, you cooperate. Story: you have felt unwell for a few weeks and feverish (you haven't measured your temperature); paracetamol hasn't helped. You returned about two weeks ago from a one-week conference in Jakarta, Indonesia. If asked about activities: you went bushwalking and ate street food; you did NOT drink unbottled water, share needles, get tattoos/piercings, or have sex overseas. On direct questioning about hepatitis features you volunteer: your eyes look yellow, your urine is dark 'tea-coloured', your stools are pale, and you have vague discomfort/pain in the upper-right/epigastric area. No weight loss, no lumps, no night sweats. You are sexually active with one regular partner and use condoms. Affect: mildly worried once the yellow eyes are mentioned; you want to know what is wrong and whether it is serious.
candidate_instructions: You are a GP at Young District Hospital (rural NSW). Tom, 34, presents feeling 'unwell' and is requesting a repeat medical certificate. In 8 minutes: take a focused history of the undifferentiated unwell/febrile patient, including a structured travel and exposure history, generate and narrow your differential, and briefly outline your provisional diagnosis and initial investigations. You do not need to complete an examination but may state what you would look for.
examiner_instructions: This tests a systematic approach to 'unwell/fever in a returned traveller' converging on acute Hepatitis A. Reward: agreeing to the certificate while safely asking questions first; clarifying 'unwell' then fever (infection until proven otherwise); a structured travel/exposure history (destination, duration, activities, contacts, drugs, exposures incl. street food and water, sexual history, pre-travel vaccines); completing the differential rather than tunnelling on the liver once jaundice features appear; and applying SOCRATES to the RUQ/epigastric discomfort. Key positives to give if asked: yellow eyes, dark urine, pale stools, RUQ discomfort, bushwalking and street food. Correct the common error - a raised WCC does NOT confirm hepatitis (WCC is usually normal/low with relative lymphocytosis). Candidate should list Hepatitis A AND E (both faeco-oral) and state Hep A is notifiable. Prompt if needed: 'All fever in a returned traveller is what until proven otherwise?'

criteria: Responds safely to the certificate request - agrees to provide it while explaining a few questions are needed to ensure safety
Clarifies 'unwell' then explores fever (measured temp, chills, timing, pattern, progression, response to paracetamol)
Takes a structured travel and exposure history (destination, duration, activities, contacts, drug use, blood exposures, food/water, sexual history, pre-travel vaccines)
Applies SOCRATES to the RUQ/epigastric discomfort and elicits hepatitis features (jaundice, dark urine, pale stools)
Completes the wider differential screen (malignancy red flags, STI, respiratory) rather than tunnelling once hepatitis is suspected
Treats fever in a returned traveller as malaria until proven otherwise and structures differential clusters
Identifies acute Hepatitis A as the provisional diagnosis with a coherent rationale (faeco-oral street food exposure)
Includes Hepatitis E in the differential (faeco-oral, endemic in the region) alongside Hep B/C
Avoids the error of interpreting a raised WCC as confirming infection/hepatitis
Requests the standard acute hepatitis serology panel (Hep A IgM, HBsAg/anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV +/- HCV RNA, Hep E IgM) plus FBE, LFTs, EBV/CMV
Interprets the hepatocellular LFT pattern (AST/ALT markedly raised) and confirms with Hepatitis A IgM
Recognises Hepatitis A is nationally notifiable - notify the public health unit; offer contacts vaccine/immunoglobulin
Supportive management and safety-net: rest, hydration, avoid alcohol/hepatotoxic drugs, hand/food hygiene, return if drowsy, confused or bleeding (fulminant hepatitis)
Non-judgemental, structured questioning and appropriate handling of the certificate request
Explains the diagnosis and plan in plain language and checks understanding

red_flags: All fever in a returned traveller is malaria until proven otherwise - requires thick and thin films
Signs of fulminant hepatitis: drowsiness, confusion (encephalopathy) or bleeding/bruising (coagulopathy)
Malignancy red flags with 'unwell': unexplained weight loss, appetite loss, lymphadenopathy, night sweats
Ascending cholangitis / biliary obstruction (fever, RUQ pain and jaundice - Charcot's triad) as a not-to-be-missed cause of jaundice
Hepatitis E in pregnancy carries a high risk of fulminant hepatic failure
australian_guidelines: Murtagh / eTG: all fever in a returned traveller is malaria until proven otherwise; first-line screening includes FBE/ESR, thick and thin films, LFTs and urine micro/culture
eTG Gastrointestinal / Australian Immunisation Handbook: Hepatitis A and E are faeco-orally transmitted; travellers to developing countries are at risk - request Hep A IgM and Hep E IgM serology

Hepatitis A is a nationally notifiable disease in Australia - notify the local public health unit; offer household/close contacts Hepatitis A vaccine or normal human immunoglobulin per the Australian Immunisation Handbook
Acute Hepatitis A management is largely supportive: rest, hydration, avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs, review medications; exclude from food-handling work while infectious
eTG/Murtagh jaundice strategy: differential includes viral hepatitis, choledocholithiasis, alcoholic hepatitis and serious causes such as pancreatic/biliary malignancy and ascending cholangitis
learning_objectives: Approach the undifferentiated 'unwell/febrile' patient with a structured differential and travel history
Take a complete ABCDE travel and exposure history in a returned traveller
Recognise the clinical and biochemical picture of acute viral hepatitis (hepatocellular LFT pattern, Hep A IgM)
Include Hepatitis E in the differential of faeco-oral traveller's hepatitis
Apply Australian public-health obligations (notifiable disease) and contact prophylaxis
key_points: In acute viral hepatitis the WCC is typically normal or low with relative/atypical lymphocytosis - a raised WCC does not confirm the diagnosis
Do not tunnel onto a liver work-up as soon as jaundice appears - complete the wider 'unwell' differential first
Hepatitis A IgM positive confirms acute Hepatitis A; a hepatocellular pattern shows AST/ALT disproportionately raised versus ALP
Hepatitis A is faeco-oral (contaminated food/water) - street food in an endemic region is the likely source; Hepatitis E shares this route
Hepatitis A is notifiable and largely self-limiting; warn about fulminant hepatitis and give food-hygiene advice

citations.claim: Hepatitis A (and E) are transmitted faeco-orally and travellers to developing countries are at risk of contracting viral hepatitis.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1363

citations.claim: Any fever in a returned traveller must be treated as malaria until proven otherwise, with first-line screening including FBE/ESR, thick and thin films, LFTs and urine micro/culture.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.3446

citations.claim: The differential for adult jaundice includes viral hepatitis, common bile duct gallstones, alcoholic hepatitis and serious causes such as pancreatic/biliary malignancy and ascending cholangitis.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1350
